The Yoga-cūḍāmaṇi Upaniṣad.
"May they swell"—thus the peace invocation.
The six limbs of yoga.
Out of a desire for the welfare of yogis, I shall proclaim the *Yogacūḍāmaṇi*,
the secret bestower of the perfection of liberation, practiced by the foremost among those who know yoga.
Posture, restraint of the breath, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, and absorption—these are the six limbs of yoga. (2)
One is declared to be Siddhāsana, the second is Kamalāsana.
Regarding the explanation:
[the breath] resides above the thousand-spoked [lotus] at the beginning of the six cakras starting from Mūlādhāra.
I worship the feet of Rāmacandra, the primary fruit of the knowledge of yoga.
Indeed, this *Yogacūḍāmaṇi Upaniṣad*, which is a division of the *Sāmaveda*,
stands preeminent as it culminates in the non-dual Brahman alone, preceded by the demonstration of the means of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*). Of this [Upaniṣad], from its brief text...
The commentary begins. With reference to the world of those ignorant of their own true nature, the Śruti says as follows:
"Yoga... etc. The meaning is that the *Yogacūḍāmaṇi* is the crest-jewel of Yoga; that is to say, it is the best among Yogas. How is its status as a crest-jewel established?
The meaning is that its being a crest-jewel is appropriate. || 1 ||

(238) For those perfected in the practice of the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) is taught; first, "posture" (*āsana*) is mentioned. Regarding the phrase "one [posture]," it is said that the definition of the Siddha-padmāsana has been elucidated in the *Triśikhibrāhmaṇopaniṣad*.
For the attainment of yoga, knowledge of the essential principles of the body is necessary:
the six chakras, the sixteen supports, the three targets, and the five voids.
"How can there be accomplishment for one who does not know his own body?"—thus he raises the objection: "Without knowledge of the reality of the body, how can there be accomplishment within the body?
[The answer begins with] "the six chakras," meaning the six chakras beginning with Mūlādhāra, starting from the triangle of Mūlādhāra.
The sixteen supports exist up to the limit of the End of the Sixteen (Ṣoḍaśānta); this is well known in the *Rājayogasāra*.

There are three objects of focus according to the division of external, internal, and intermediate. The five voids consist of the space [element] and so forth, ending with the Supreme Space (*paramākāśa*). The remainder is clear.
The cakras beginning with the mūlādhāra are as follows: the ādhāra has four petals, and the svādhiṣṭhāna has six petals.
At the navel is a ten-petaled lotus; at the heart, a twelve-spoked [wheel];
the one called Viśuddha has sixteen spokes; and likewise, between the eyebrows, there is a two-petaled [lotus].
Regarding that which was asked by you— the [lotus] numbered as having a thousand petals at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) on the great path—
he says, "the four-petaled [lotus]," etc., meaning that it is included within the range from the mūlādhāra up to the end of the thousand-spoked [lotus]. (4–5)
The vision of the supreme light at the place of the womb is the first wheel, the foundation; the second is the Svādhiṣṭhāna. || 6 ||
The place of the womb (yonisthāna) between the two is called Kāmarūpa;
however, that which is named Kāma is the four-petalled lotus situated in the region of the anus.
In the center of that, the Yoni named Kāmākhya, worshipped by the Siddhas, is proclaimed;
in its center stands the Great Liṅga, facing the west. (8)
He who knows the jewel-like image at the navel— shining like molten gold and flashing like a streak of lightning— is a knower of Yoga.
That city of fire is triangular and is established below the genitals;
in meditative absorption, it is the supreme light, infinite and facing in all directions.
When that great yoga is seen, coming and going no longer exist.
He explains [the sequence] in order, designating the names of the first and second wheels:
"The support," etc. (verse 6). Regarding what the place of the womb (*yonisthāna*) is, he says: "The place of the womb. Of the two...

Regarding the *mūlādhāra* and *svādhiṣṭhāna*: since the attainment of yoga is preceded by their pressure, he clarifies that very point with the words "called Kāmā" (*kāmākhyam*). [It is] called Kāmā because it is the desire for the attainment of yoga. (7) The *yoni* is the power *Kuṇḍalinī*. Her status as a *yoni* is established because she is the cause of the birth of the universe. For this very reason...

Kāmākhyā: In the center of the coils of Kuṇḍalinī, which shines within the middle of the Suṣumnā, there exists the great Liṅga of Vāyu, facing westward; it becomes perceptible to the yogi through the practice of *kevala-kumbhaka* alone. (8) Thus, he states the fruit of practice for one possessing such knowledge:

"Blazing" (taptā) || 9 || He says that for one who thus perceives the fiery flame at the time of yoga, there is no longer any coming and going by way of the paths of iḍā and so forth— this is stated in the verse beginning with "in samādhi" (samādhau) || 10 ||
Regarding the characteristics of the wheels (cakras) beginning with Svādhiṣṭhāna:
by the word "sva" (self), there is the vital breath (prāṇa); that which is its support is the Svādhiṣṭhāna.
Because it is the locus of one's own self-perfection (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), this very [organ] is called the penis;
for here, the bulbous root (*kanda*) is threaded by the *suṣumṇā* like a gem with a thread.
In the circle of its navel, the wheel called Maṇipūraka is proclaimed;
it is a great wheel with twelve spokes, free from merit and demerit. (13)

The individual soul (jīva) wanders in this manner only so long as it does not find the reality characterized by its own locus (svādhiṣṭhāna). He states [the definition of] "its own" with the word "sva" [in the verse]. Because the penis is the channel for vital breath (prāṇa), its status as the locus of the svādhiṣṭhāna is appropriate. [Now follows] the definition of the maṇipūraka.

"Why [is it] not by means of a thread here? (12). He states that the individual soul (*jīva*), seated in the heart, wanders through the circle of transmigratory existence until its own ignorance ceases—[this is shown in the verse] "The twelve-spoked" and so forth. In that [wheel], which is devoid of merit and demerit, there is an absence of connection with merit and demerit for one who perceives the inward Self (*pratyagdṛṣṭi*).
The great wheel of the channels (nāḍī-mahācakra) is above the penis and below the navel; it is the source of the bulb (kanda-yoni), like the interior of a bird's egg.
Therein, seventy-two thousand channels have arisen;
among those thousands of channels, seventy-two are specifically mentioned. (15)
Among those, ten are traditionally held to be the principal channels for the flow of vital breath;
they are Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā as the third.
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, and the illustrious Pūṣā; Alambusā and Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is recorded as the tenth. (17)
This great wheel of channels (nāḍī-mahācakra) should always be known by yogins.
He describes the bulb of the channels (nāḍī-kanda) and the divisions of the channels situated therein, beginning with the word "upward" (ūrdhvam). || 14-15 ||
He indicates the locations of the ten channels with the words "Iḍā" etc. (verses 16–17).
Regarding the locations of the channels:
*iḍā* is situated on the left side, and *piṅgalā* is situated on the right. (18)
Suṣumnā is in the middle region, Gāndhārī is in the left eye, Hastijihvā is in the right [eye], and Pūṣā is in the right ear. (19)
Yaśasvinī is in the left ear, and Alambusā is also in the face;
Kuhū is in the region of the genitals, while Śaṅkhinī is in the location of the root.
Thus, the channels (nāḍīs) stand in succession, relying upon the gates;
of those situated in the center, the Suṣumnā, the Iḍā is located on the left.
The winds that circulate through the channels and their functions—the Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā—reside within the pathways of the vital breath (prāṇa). || 21 ||
Constantly flowing as the carriers of the vital breath are the deities Soma, Sūrya, and Agni;
these are the winds known as prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, and udāna.
The *nāga*, *kūrma*, *kṛkara*, *devadatta*, and *dhanañjaya* [are the five winds];
*prāṇa* is eternally situated in the heart, and *apāna* is in the region of the anus. (23)
The *samāna* wind is located at the region of the navel, while the *udāna* resides in the middle of the throat; the *vyāna* pervades the entire body—these are the five principal winds. (24)
Nāga is said to be in the act of belching; likewise, Kūrma is in the opening of the eyes.
Kṛkara is to be known as that which produces hunger, and Devadatta is in yawning. (25)
Even when one has died, the all-pervading Dhanañjaya does not abandon [the body].
These living beings wander through all the channels (nāḍīs). (26)

In that context, regarding the distinction between the non-yogi and the yogi, [it is said] "the *iḍā*": || 21 || He describes the nature of the *prāṇa* and other [winds] residing in the channels (*nāḍī*) and their functions: "the *prāṇa*... || 22–25 || "Living beings" (*jīvajantu*) means those whose form is the individual soul (*jīva*), because [the channels] serve as the substratum for their life-force. || 26 ||
Just as a ball rises when impelled by the movement or stillness of the arm,
so too the individual soul (jīva) does not remain stationary when impelled by the vital breaths (prāṇa and apāna). || 27 ||
The individual soul, under the sway of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, indeed runs upward and downward;
because of its flickering nature through the left and right paths, it is not perceived. (28)

Just as a hawk bound by a string is drawn back even though it has flown away, so too the individual soul (jīva), bound by the qualities (guṇas), is pulled along by the out-breath and in-breath (prāṇa-apāna). || 29 ||
Under the influence of the prāṇa and apāna, the living being indeed moves upward and downward;
the apāna draws up the prāṇa, and the prāṇa draws up the apāna.
He who knows these two situated above and below is a knower of yoga.

He states that the movement or non-movement of the individual soul (jīva) is dependent upon the movement or non-movement of the vital breath (prāṇa)—[this is expressed in the verse beginning] "ākṣipta" (27).
He clarifies that very point [in the verses beginning] "prāṇa" (28–30).
(343) The contemplation of the Ajapā Gāyatrī:
by the letter *ha* it goes out, and by the letter *sa* it enters again. || 31 ||
The individual soul (jīva) constantly recites this mantra, "Haṃsa, Haṃsa," six hundred times by day and twenty-one thousand times by night. (32)
The individual soul constantly recites this mantra endowed with this number;
it is known as Ajapā Gāyatrī, which always bestows liberation upon yogis.
By the mere resolve for this [mantra], one is liberated from all sins;
there is no knowledge equal to this, and no recitation equal to this. (34)
There has never been, nor will there ever be, knowledge equal to this:
the Gāyatrī, the sustainer of life, which has arisen within the Kuṇḍalinī. (35)
The science of the vital breath (prāṇavidyā) is the great science; he who knows it is a knower of the Vedas.

The activity of the prāṇa, apāna, exhalation, and so forth, is indeed the Haṃsa-mantra. Since the Ajapā-Gāyatrī is brought about by the living being itself, he states its extent and the fruit of knowing it with the words beginning "By the letter 'Ha'."

31-33 || By maintaining the awareness of the *ajapā* [mantra] "haṃsaḥ so 'ham" (I am He) during inhalation and exhalation, the individual soul (*jīva*) is liberated from all sins. He praises the *ajapā* with the words "by this" [verse 34]. [Verse 34: "By this...
He states the fruit of knowledge—that the *ajapā* is born from the *kuṇḍalinī*—with the words "in the *kuṇḍalinī*" [verse 35]. [Verse 35: "In the *kuṇḍalinī*..."
The piercing of the door of liberation by Kuṇḍalinī:
above the *kanda*, the power Kuṇḍalī is eightfold and coiled in shape. || 36 ||
The gateway of Brahman remains eternally covered by a mouth;
through that gateway one must go to the stainless gateway of Brahman. (37)
Having covered that door with her mouth, the Supreme Goddess fell asleep;
she was awakened by the union with fire, together with the mind and the vital breath. (38)
Taking hold of the body through the *suṣumnā*, he ascends as easily as one might go upward;
just as one opens the door of a house with a key, so the yogi shall break open the door of liberation by means of the *kuṇḍalinī*. (39)
Having joined the hands in the *saṃpuṭita* gesture and firmly assumed the *padmāsana* posture, one should place the chin tightly against the chest, perform the meditation upon that [breath],
and repeatedly exhale the filled *apāna* wind upwards.
Releasing his vital breath, a man attains incomparable awakening through the power of Śakti.
Having massaged his limbs with water produced from physical exertion,
he should abstain from pungent, sour, and salty foods and subsist on a diet of milk.
A practitioner of yoga who observes celibacy, eats moderately, and is devoted to yoga shall become a perfected being after one year; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. || 42 ||
Eating very smooth and sweet food with one-fourth of the portion remaining,
out of devotion to Śiva— he is called a "moderate eater" (mitāhārī).
Above the *kanda* is the power Kuṇḍalī, coiled eightfold;
she is the cause of bondage for the ignorant, yet always the bestower of liberation upon yogins. (44)

(p. 345) He describes the nature of Kuṇḍalinī, who is the support of all living beings, and her activity—beginning with the verse "In the *kanda*... (36). [The passage] "the mouth of the Brahma-door called Suṣumnā" (37) refers to the opening of the Brahma-door. [The passage] "asleep in the region of the Mūlādhāra for those who are not yogins; awakened at the time of yoga for yogins" (38) indicates that she is dormant in the region of the Mūlādhāra for non-yogins, but becomes awakened during the practice of yoga for yogins. This is because...

This [power] is skillful at breaking open the door to liberation; therefore, just as one uses a key for the bolt of a temple, the yogin should break open the door to liberation by means of it—thus he says, "he should unlock. (39)
He states the means for that differentiation and its fruit, beginning with "having done": the practitioner, a yogin,
having joined his two hands together in a hollowed gesture (saṃpuṭita) level with his own heart, having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana),
and having firmly placed his chin against his chest—

Having applied the Jālandhara-bandha, characterized by the contraction of the throat, one should repeatedly draw the Apana upward with the Mūla-bandha; once filled with air, one should project it upward and lead it into union with the Prana. Following that union, one should maintain the Kevala-kumbhaka.

By the power of the Kuṇḍalinī energy, abandoning the activity of that Kuṇḍalinī—the operation of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth—and having performed meditation and reflection upon "I am Brahman," which is free from the conceptualization of the three bodies, he attains perfect awakening; at that very moment, he reaches the Prāṇa, which is the Supreme Self (paramātman). Thus.
He states that the yogi who practices the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) becomes perfected without delay: "Of the limbs," etc.

The meaning is that if perspiration arises during the time of practice, then by means of water, one's body shall become firm. He describes the rule for food conducive to yoga: "Pungent," etc. (41–43).
He says that this power (*śakti*) may be the cause of both bondage and liberation for those who are unyoked and those who are yoked—starting with the word "kanda":
if she resides in the lower part of the *kanda*, then she leads to bondage; if she has gone upward from the *kanda* by way of the path of the *suṣumnā*, then she bestows liberation upon yogins. (44)
He who knows the three bandhas— mahāmudrā, nabhomudrā, and oḍyāṇa, as well as jalaṃdhara and mūlabandha— is a yogin who becomes a vessel for liberation. 45.
Having pressed firmly with the heel, one should contract the perineum;
drawing the *apāna* upward, this is called *mūlabandha*. (46)
Through the unification of the *apāna* and *prāṇa* breaths and the exhaustion of urine and feces, even an old man becomes young through the constant practice of *mūlabandha*. (47)
Because the great bird performs its flight there without ceasing, that very place is Oḍḍiyāṇa, the lion to the elephant of death. 48.
The protection situated behind the abdomen, below the navel, is called Oḍyāṇa;
the binding of the abdomen is the "bandha" prescribed therein. (49)
For it binds the water from the sky that flows downward toward the head;
therefore, the Jālandhara band destroys the multitude of afflictions in the throat. (50)
When the Jālandhara-bandha is performed, which destroys the flood of suffering in the throat, the nectar does not fall into the fire, nor does the breath rush upward. (51)

He says, "Mahāmudrā" (verse 45), [meaning] that one becomes a partaker of liberation through the knowledge of the Mahāmudrā and so forth to be described hereafter. He states the definition of the Mūlabandha and other [postures] in "Pārṣṇi" (verse 46).
This is the result of that: "The downward breath," and so forth. (47–52)
When the tongue enters the hollow of the skull and is turned upward,
and the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows, that is the Khecarī Mudrā. (52)
For him who knows the Khecarī Mudrā, there is neither disease nor death, neither sleep, hunger, nor thirst; nor shall he ever suffer from fainting. (53)
He who knows the Khecarī Mudrā is not afflicted by disease, is not stained by karma, and is not bound by anything whatsoever. (54)
Because the mind moves in the void and because the tongue moves in the void, this is the Khecarī Mudrā, saluted by all the Siddhas. || 55 ||
The channels, which have their root in the *bindu*, are established there;
they nourish the bodies from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
For one by whom the opening above the uvula is sealed by the *khecarī* [mudrā],
his seminal essence (*bindu*) does not waste away, even when embraced by a passionate woman.
As long as the bindu remains in the body, whence can there be fear of death? As long as the mudrā of space is bound, the bindu does not depart. (58)

This is the fruit of that; it is not a disease. (53–55) He says—beginning with "the bindu"—that yogins established in the khecarīmudrā perceive everything within the body. By the word *sirā*, the channels (*nāḍīs*) are meant.
The *bindu* is indeed the Lord (*īśvara*), in whom the fourteen worlds characterized by those [channels] are established.

The roots of those infinite millions of cosmic eggs are the *bindu*; those bodies— the infinite millions of cosmic eggs— a yogi established in the *khecarīmudrā* contemplates as his own body, from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head, in the state of the Great Virāj.
The meaning is "they lead. Furthermore—[it is said] "by Khecarī" [verse 57]. The meaning is that the Sky-Seal (nabhomudrā) is Khecarī [verse 58].

The characteristic of the yogi of Vajrolī and other [mudrās] is as follows: even though the drop (bindu) has blazed up and reached the fire, it goes upward when it has ascended by means of the power (śakti) and is restrained by the Yonimudrā. || 59 ||
Furthermore, that *bindu* is of two kinds: white and likewise red.
They call the white one "semen" (*śukla*), and that which is named red is "great passion" (*mahārāga*). (60)
The quality of passion (rajas), resembling a mass of vermilion, resides in the station of the sun;
the pure quality (sattva) resides in the station of the moon; the unification of these two is very difficult to attain.
The *bindu* is Brahmā, and the *rajas* is Śakti; the *bindu* is the moon, and the *rajas* is the sun.
Only through the union of these two is the supreme state attained. (62)
Just as dust is driven by the wind that stirs the power (śakti), so the bindu always attains oneness; then one possesses a divine body.
The white [element] is conjoined with the moon, and the rajas is accompanied by the sun;
he who knows the state of their equal flavor and unity is a knower of yoga. 64.

He states the characteristics of the yogi, such as the *vajrolī* practitioner, with the words "even when ignited" (*jvalito’pi*). Just as a drop of metal-melting agent ignites upon contact with iron, so too this *bindu*, even when ignited by the proximity of a woman, consumes the semen offered by the man; thus, it is called *hutāśana*. This occurs even when it has entered the circle of the female womb (*yonimaṇḍala*).

The meaning is that, being restrained by the power of the *yonimudrā*, characterized by the contraction of the *liṅga*, it moves only upwards and does not fall downwards according to one's strength. The sense is that because this *amaroli-yoga* has been mastered, that *bindu* never leaks. (59–60)
In the regions above the circle of the eyebrows, on the left and right sides, are the positions of the sun and the moon.

The meaning is that the union of the sun and the moon, which consist of the forms of *rajas* and *śukla*, is difficult for anyone other than a yogin to attain. Furthermore—“the *bindu*... (verse 62). By whom [is this union of the sun and the moon achieved]?

To the question, "What is produced by that?", he says: "By the wind. Just as dust, being impelled by a fierce wind through the movement of its own power, attains oneness with the sun, so too the *rajas* situated in the lunar orb—impelled by the movement of the power of Kuṇḍalinī together with the wind—is called the *bindu*.

The nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental; [the yogin] always attains oneness with the Bindu and the Sun (p. 349). When the union of the Sun and the Moon occurs, then this yogin becomes possessed of a divine body. || 63-64 ||
The purification of the network of channels, the movement of the moon and sun, and the drying up of the fluids— this indeed is designated as Mahāmudrā. (65)
Placing the chin upon the chest, pressing the vulva for a long time with the left foot while holding the extended right foot with both hands,
and filling both sides of the abdomen with breath, one should exhale slowly after binding [the breath].
This very great mudrā is said to be the destroyer of diseases for human beings. || 66 ||
Having practiced with the lunar portion, one should practice again with the solar portion;
when the count has become equal, then one should release the mudrā.
Neither wholesome nor unwholesome—indeed, all tastes become flavorless;
even terrible poison, when consumed in excess, is digested as if it were nectar. 68.
For one who practices Mahāmudrā, diseases such as consumption, leprosy, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, and indigestion go to their destruction. (69)
This Mahāmudrā, which brings about great accomplishment for human beings, has been taught; it must be guarded with effort and not given to just anyone. (70)
He describes the true nature of Mahāmudrā and its fruit, beginning with the word "purification":
that which effects the purification of the channels, which sets in motion both the moon and the sun,
and which acts as a desiccant for the corrupted humors such as wind and bile residing within the body— that indeed [is it].

This is designated as Mahāmudrā. As for the method of its practice: first, having applied the Jālandhara-bandha and pressing the *yoni* with the sole of the left foot, one holds the right leg extended outward while supporting it with both hands.

Having filled both the left and right sides of the abdomen with the breath arising from the *candranāḍī* (left channel), and having bound it without exhaling, one should slowly exhale through the *piṅgalā* (right channel) at the end of the *kumbhaka*.
This very practice is the *mahāmudrā*, which destroys all diseases of men. Thus...
"By a portion of the moon," etc. (67–70).

Having ascended the lotus posture (padmāsana) with the body, head, and neck held straight, and with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose, one should mutter the imperishable syllable Om (praṇava) in a solitary place.

Having thus practiced Mahāmudrā, one should then constantly recite the Praṇava according to the prescribed method, preceded by a contemplation on the meaning of the Praṇava; thus it is said: "In the lotus" refers to Brahman, whose nature is the meaning of the Praṇava.

Oṃ. That which is eternal, pure, awakened, free from conceptual construction, stainless, ineffable, without beginning or end, the one, the fourth state (*turīya*), that which has been, is, and will be, that which revolves, which is at all times uninterrupted—the Supreme Brahman. From that, the *parā* [was born].

Śakti herself is of the nature of self-luminous light. From the Self, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; and from water, earth. The lords of these five elements are the five: Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā. Of these...

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the agents of creation, preservation, and dissolution; Brahmā is of the nature of *rajas*, Viṣṇu is of the nature of *sattva*, and Rudra is of the nature of *tamas*. These three are endowed with the [three] qualities (*guṇas*). Brahmā was born as the first among the gods;
Dhātṛ is for creation, Viṣṇu for preservation, and Rudra for destruction and enjoyment.

Candra was the first-born. From these, the worlds of Brahmā arise—the gods, animals, humans, and stationary beings. For those such as humans, the body is a composite of the five elements. Through the organs of knowledge and action, [knowledge is attained]—

That too is called the gross nature (*sthūla-prakṛti*). Although it abides in the subtle, it is called the "liṅga" (the subtle body) because of the organs of knowledge and action, the objects of knowledge, the five vital airs beginning with *prāṇa*, the mind, and the intellect.
It is the cause endowed with the three qualities (*guṇas*). Thus, for all beings, these three bodies exist.
There are four states: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turiya). The presiding lords of these states are the four persons:
Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, and Ātman.
For Viśva always experiences the gross; Taijasa experiences the subtle; likewise, Prājña experiences bliss; and beyond that is the Witness of All.
The Praṇava should always abide within all living beings through experience;
it is indeed delightful in all states, yet facing downwards.
He states that the consciousness which is the meaning of the syllable *Oṃ* is Brahman, saying "Om.
Since the words such as "eternally pure" (*nityaśuddha*) have been explained word by word in the *Nṛsiṃhatāpanīya*, [it is understood].
"Being" (*bhūta*) means that it exists by itself in a single form throughout the three periods of time, beginning with the past.

The meaning is that Brahman is the consciousness which is the referent of the syllable *praṇava*— that which is without beginning or end because it is devoid of origination and dissolution, and which is uninterrupted and free from limitation.
If Brahman is its own absolute nature, devoid of any counterpart, then from where does the creation— from the unmanifest down to stationary objects— arise?

Anticipating this doubt, he says "tasmāt" (therefore), meaning that all this appears as born from that [Brahman] due to ignorance of it. From that non-dual Brahman— which, from the perspective of one's own ignorance,
is the undifferentiated Brahman that is its own absolute self alone, devoid of any counter-correlate— [all this arises].

The supreme power (*parā śakti*), whose nature is universal consciousness (*citsāmānyātmikā*), appears as if born—though not in reality—due to the proximity of the substratum for its own superimposition and negation; she is essentially self-luminous (*svayaṃjyotirātmikā*). Thus, [she arises] from the Self (*ātman*) which is conditioned by the unmanifest (*avyakta*) and the principle of the Great One (*mahattattva*), both of which are conceptualized through the vision of one's own ignorance (*svājñadṛṣṭi*). Thus, from the Self...
From that [source], the five elements were produced in succession; of these, and so forth.
How is it that the agency in creation and so on is caused by the conjunction with the three *guṇas*? [The text says]: "It is *rājasa*. (p.
352) Brahmā and the others, who are the agents of creation and so forth, have attained the state of being first-born.

Thus he says: "Brahman. For the Śruti states: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning. Regarding that, [the text says] "He who is the Creator" and so forth. That which in the beginning arose as the one Being-consciousness (sac-caitanya) is itself, in accordance with the various effects such as creation and so on, [designated by these names].
The meaning is that because he shines as having attained the state of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra, his status as the first-born among them is stated. Among these, "of Brahmā," and so forth:
from Brahmā [proceed] the fourteen worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, as well as the gods, animals, and humans who dwell therein, as objects of his enjoyment.
Immobile beings and immobile things are born. Regarding their body, he says "of them," meaning that their body is composed of the elements (bhautika).

With reference to the individual soul (jīva) as it ascends through states such as waking and so forth, he demonstrates the three bodies in accordance with those respective states—beginning with "knowledge" (jñāna)—by means of objects.

That which is qualified by the grossly conceived effects of the fivefold elements (*pañcīkṛtabhūta*) is also the *jīva*. The meaning is that the *viśva* is the one characterized by the gross body as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), which identifies with the waking state.

He describes the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) as the object of experience for the *taijasa*: "by means of knowledge," etc.; [it is] by means of the effects of the non-fivefold elements (*apañcīkṛtabhūta*).
The *taijasa* (the luminous self), conjoined with knowledge, its objects, and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) along with the intellect (*buddhi*),

though abiding in the subtle— that is, residing in the subtle body— during the state of dream, is called "merely the *liṅga*" (the subtle body) because of its non-difference from it. That which is brought about by the *prājña* (the conscious self) who identifies with deep sleep...

The cause endowed with the three qualities (guṇas) constitutes the causal body (kāraṇa-śarīra). He states that Viśva and the other triad possess the state of being the enjoyers of the gross and so forth, while the Fourth (turīya) is devoid of that—thus [he says] "Viśva" etc. (verse 72).
He states the all-pervasiveness of the fourth *praṇava* with the words "the *praṇava*":

the *praṇava*, the fourth *oṃkāra*, which is the fourth witness (*sākṣī*), always abides in the form of the inner self (*pratyag-rūpa*) within all living beings who have attained the states of Viśva and the others due to the conceit of enjoyment associated with the grossly differentiated [levels] and so forth. It abides on all sides.

It is called *abhirāma* because it shines and is glorified on all sides. The fourth state, however, remains indifferent—looking downward and turned away—in all states such as waking and the rest, due to its perception of their falsity;
the meaning is that, unlike the *viśva* and other states, it never faces toward the waking state and so forth. || 73 ||

The meaning of each of the constituent parts of the *praṇava*—the three phonemes *a*, *u*, and *m*—is as follows: they are the three Vedas, the three worlds, the three qualities (*guṇas*), and the three syllables; thus does the *praṇava* manifest.
The syllable *a* exists in all living beings during the waking state in the eyes;
the syllable *u* is in the throat during dreaming; and the syllable *m* is in the heart during deep sleep. (74)

The letter *a* is Virāṭ, Viśva, the gross, and the waking state; the letter *u* is Hiraṇyagarbha, Taijasa, the subtle, and the dreaming state; the letter *m* is the Unmanifest Cause, Prājña, and the state of deep sleep.
The letter *a* is said to be of the nature of *rajas*, red, Brahmā, and consciousness.
The syllable *U* is characterized by sattva, is white in color, and is designated as Viṣṇu. || 75 ||
The letter *ma* is characterized by *tamas*, is black, and is likewise called Rudra;
from the *praṇava* originates Brahmā, and from the *praṇava* originates Hari.
Rudra originates from the Praṇava, for the Praṇava is indeed supreme;
Brahmā dissolves into the syllable *A*, and Hari dissolves into the syllable *U*.
In the letter *ma*, Rudra dissolves; indeed, the *praṇava* shines forth.
He says that the entire collection of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is beyond one's own self, is produced from the constituent parts of the *praṇava*: "The letter *a*," and so on.
There are three—that is, three syllables. Thus, in reality, the *praṇava* always shines forth.
Regarding how the vowels beginning with *a* are all-pervasive, it is said here: "The letter *a*... (verses 74–75).
He states that the fourth state (turiya) alone is the substratum for the superimposition and negation of Brahma and the rest, beginning with the word "praṇavāt" (from the syllable Om). || 76 ||
Rudra, and then the Praṇava. || 77 ||
May this Brahman, illuminated at the peak of the fourth *oṃkāra*, ascend upward for the wise, but remain downward-facing for the ignorant. (78)
Thus indeed should one abide as the Praṇava; he who knows it is a knower of the Veda.
By way of its unstruck (anāhata) nature, it becomes the upward-moving path for the wise.
Like an unbroken stream of oil, like the resonance of a long-sounding bell—such is the sound of the *praṇava*; its apex is called Brahman. (80)
That peak consists of light and is inexpressible due to the subtlety of the intellect;
those great-souled ones who have seen it—he who knows that is a knower of the Veda. (81)

He says that one who knows that the *praṇava* alone shines forth—appearing as facing upward and downward according to the perspectives of the knower of the Self and the non-knower of the Self—is a knower of the Veda; this is expressed by the words "of the knowers.
From the perspective of the knower, [it shines] in the form of Brahman, which is non-different from the inner self (*pratyak*) manifesting in the *anāhata* [cakra].

The Praṇava shines above all as nothing but Brahman, illuminated at the tip of the fourth state (turīya); the meaning is that it appears to the ignorant as having a downward-facing form and so forth. Furthermore: "In oil... [etc. || 80-81 ||
The Haṃsa, which is the fourth state—the meaning of the Praṇava—shines as the very Haṃsa between the two eyes while awake.
The letter *sa* is declared to be Khecarī and is certainly the *tvaṃ-pada*. (72)
The letter *ha* is the Supreme Lord, and it is certain that it is his state;
when the living being meditates upon the letter *sa*, he shall certainly become the letter *ha*.
The living being is bound by the senses, but the Self is not bound at all. Through the sense of "mine-ness" one becomes a living being; through the absence of "mine-ness," one is liberated.
Regarding the question of where the *haṃsa*—the fourth state which is the meaning of the *praṇava*—resides and shines forth, it is said:

"The relationship of support and supported is heard [in scripture]. Thus, between the two eyes of the waking state, which consist of support and supported, the *haṃsa* is none other than the Supreme Self non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*), serving as the locus for the superimposition and negation of those [states].
It shines forth. From what source does the *haṃsa* possess its nature as the inner self (*pratyaktva*), its nature as the supreme (*paratva*), or the established unity of these two?

To this, he says: "The letter *sa*. Because it moves in reverse order through the *liṅgaśarīra*, which is the form of the supreme (*parā*) located there within the *kha*—the unmanifest space (*avyākṛtākāśa*) existing in the hearts of all living beings—it is called *khecarī*.

The letter *sa* is said to be [the seed-syllable] because *sa* is the seed of Khecarī; for it has been stated by the Lord that "that is the meaning of the term *tvaṃ*. Therefore, it is certain that the seed-syllable *sa* is the immediate consciousness (*pratyak-caitanya*) which is the meaning of the term *tvaṃ*. The meaning of the letter *ha* is the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Therefore, [it is the meaning] of the seed-syllable *ha*.

It is certain that this is the supreme self-consciousness (paramātma-caitanya), which is the indicated meaning (lakṣya) of that word [Tat]. Thus, if the individual being— the living soul (jīva)— denoted by the word "Sa" (That), having cast off its own inherent state of being a living soul,
meditates upon itself as "I am the Supreme Self, non-different from the inner self (pratyagātman) indicated by the word 'Aham' (I)," [then it attains liberation].

The meaning is that when one knows [the letter *ha*], then the meaning of *ha* must be the Supreme Self alone; this is "certainly true" (dhruvaṃ satyam), according to the Vedic scripture: "One who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself. (83) He states that the presence or absence of the sense of "I" and "mine" (*ahaṃ-mama-abhimāna*) regarding the body, senses, and so forth, are the causes for the distinction or non-distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*). He says:
The recitation of the Praṇava, which illuminates the absolute Self alone:
"Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ—these worlds, whose presiding deities are the Moon, the Sun, and Fire, abide within its measures; that supreme light is Om. (85)
Will, action, and likewise knowledge—Brāhmī, Raudrī, and Vaiṣṇavī—the state of the three measures (mātrās) wherein that supreme light resides is "Om. 86.
One should constantly recite that with speech, practice it with the body,
and constantly recite it with the mind— that supreme light which is "Om."
Whether pure or impure, whoever constantly recites the *praṇava* is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
He points out the nature of the *praṇava*, which reveals the absolute Self alone—“*Bhūḥ*,” [verse 85].

He states that the supreme light is the meaning of the *praṇava*—“by speech,” [verse 87]. Having first demonstrated the absence of requirements such as ritual purity for the recitation of the *praṇava*, he declares its fruit—“pure,” [verse 88].

Even for one who practices the *praṇava*, the conquest of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is essential: "When the wind is moving, the drop (*bindu*) moves; when it is motionless, the drop becomes motionless.
The yogi attains the state of a pillar (immobility); therefore, he should restrain the wind. (89)
As long as the vital air remains in the body, so long the living soul does not depart. Death is its exit; therefore, one should restrain the vital air. (90)
As long as the wind is bound within the body, so long the life-force does not depart;
as long as the gaze remains between the eyebrows, whence can there be fear of death? (91)
Out of fear of even a short duration [of worldly existence], Brahmā became devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma);
likewise, yogins and sages should therefore restrain their vital breaths.

Having raised the objection that since the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*) are accomplished through the practice of the *praṇava*, what is the use of conquering the vital breath (*prāṇa*), [the author] replies that because the *bindu* and the *prāṇa* are mutually dependent, one must conquer the *prāṇa* for the sake of conquering the *bindu*, which is the cause of life;
thus he says: "Moving... (vv. 89–91). For this very reason, even Brahmā and the others...
He says that they become intent upon breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the words "alpa" etc.; because they become intent upon breath control, therefore [the result follows]. || 92 ||
Through the purification of the channels, there is mastery over *prāṇāyāma*.
The *haṃsa* (the vital breath) travels outward for twenty-six finger-breadths via the left and right paths; thus is *prāṇāyāma* prescribed.
When the entire wheel of channels, which was previously cluttered with impurities, becomes pure,
at that very moment the yogi becomes capable of mastering the vital breath.
He states that *prāṇāyāma* is indeed the cessation of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), saying "twenty-six":

the meaning is that the *prāṇa* flows outward along the paths of the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* for a distance of twenty-six finger-breadths; *prāṇāyāma* is prescribed for the purpose of obstructing that movement. || 93 ||
He states that after the purification of the channels, the power of *kevalakumbhaka* arises: "Purification...
(p. 357). The characteristic of *prāṇāyāma* is as follows:
the yogi, having assumed the *baddhapadmāsana*, should fill the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by means of the moon.
Or one should retain [the breath] according to one's capacity, and then exhale further through the solar [nāḍī]. || 95 ||
Having meditated upon the orb of the moon, which resembles an ocean of nectar and is comparable to the whiteness of cow’s milk, one shall become happy through breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 96 ||

Having meditated upon the solar orb, which is throbbing, blazing with flickering flames, and worthy of worship, situated within the heart, the yogi shall become happy through breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 97 ||
Regarding the characteristics of *prāṇāyāma*, he describes the two objects of meditation there as "bound," etc.
(verse 95)—namely, the purification of the channels (*nāḍīśodhana*).
If one should drink the breath through the *iḍā* [left nostril] while it is restrained, one should subsequently exhale it in the opposite manner.
Having inhaled through the Piṅgalā and then bound [the breath], one should exhale through the Vāmā;
by this method, for the self-controlled practitioner who meditates on the two drops of the Sun and Moon,
the multitude of channels becomes purified after two months.
The retention of breath as desired, the kindling of the internal fire, the manifestation of the inner sound (nāda), and freedom from disease arise from the purification of the channels. 99.
He states the means for purifying the channels: "The vital breath," etc. (98). Its fruit is: "As desired," etc.
Prāṇāyāma preceded by the regulation of measure (mātrā) consists of holding the breath as long as the prāṇa residing in the body restrains the apāna;
a single measure consists of one breath, remaining in the space above and below. (100)
Exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka), consisting of the Praṇava, thus constitute breath control (prāṇāyāma) when joined with twelve measures (mātrās). || 101 ||
The Moon and the Sun, joined with twelve measures, constantly binding the net of the defects, should always be known by yogis. (102)
One should perform twelve counts for inhalation (pūraka), sixteen for retention (kumbhaka), and ten for exhalation (recaka); that is called a *prāṇāyāma* consisting of the syllable Oṃ.
In the lowest [grade], there are twelve mātrās; in the middling, it is considered double that; in the highest, it is declared to be triple: such is the determination of prāṇāyāma. (104)
In the lowest [stage], there is the production of sweat; in the middle, trembling occurs;
in the highest, one attains the state [of steadiness]; therefore, one should restrain the vital air (vāyu). || 105 ||

The yogi, having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) and having paid homage to the Guru who is Śiva, should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) alone, with his gaze fixed on the tip of the nose. 106.

Having firmly closed the nine gates and bound the vital breath, having brought it to a firm concentration, and having moved the time-element together with the downward breath and fire by means of the power equally;
being endowed with meditation on the Self, one should, by this method, place [the breath] steadily upon the head.
As long as one remains [in the world], the association with the great is not fully praised. || 107 ||
Thus, prāṇāyāma becomes the fire that consumes the fuel of sin;
it is always described by yogis as the great bridge across the ocean of worldly existence. 108.

He states the limit for the *mūlabandha*, the definition of the *mātrā*, and the definition of *prāṇāyāma* by way of another method, beginning with the word "prāṇa. The meaning is that the duration of a natural inhalation and exhalation constitutes the time of one *mātrā*. (100–101)
(Yoginīsaṃcāra-tantra, p. 359) It is said that the yogin should meditate upon the moon and sun as ornaments of twelve *mātrās*:

"The time of the *mātrā*s. Joined with those [twelve *mātrās*], the moon and sun perform their coming and going through the lunar and solar channels (*nāḍīs*). The mention of "night" and "day" is intended as an illustration for the non-grasping of faults.
Those who bind the net of defects, being unremitting day and night, must first be understood by yogis.

Having known the movement of the lunar and solar channels (*nāḍī*), when whichever channel flows, one should perform inhalation (*pūraka*) through that [channel] and, having restrained it, perform exhalation (*recaka*) through the other. When this is done, [the breath] enters both channels of the wind.
The movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) would become even; the sense is that, consequently, breath control (prāṇāyāma) would occur without effort.
102. Then one should perform the *pūraka* (inhalation) for twelve measures; "ten *oṃ*s" means a duration of ten measures. 103. Furthermore—[regarding] the inferior [method]: 104.
Having completely restrained the vital air (*māruta*) which is accompanied by the *apāna* fire and moved together with the power of *kuṇḍalinī*, [one should hold it].

Having bound [the breath] and led it sequentially through the six cakras beginning with the *mūlādhāra* according to this method, one should place Kāla, whose nature is the fourth state (*turyātman*), upon the thousand-spoked wheel at the crown of the head; having contemplated him as stable,
for as long as he remains steady at the crown, the company of the great ones is not merely praised.
For one who has directly realized the fourth state (*turya*) at the crown of the head, there is no longer any desire for association due to having accomplished all that was to be done.

The meaning is that as long as one does not perceive the self of the fourth state within the *sahasrāra*, so long is association with the great ones praised. (Verses 106–107) He praises *prāṇāyāma* [as follows]: "Prāṇa... etc.
It is called the "Great Bridge. || 108 ||
The individual fruit of each of the limbs of yoga and their respective gradations are as follows:
by means of *āsana*, the yogi destroys physical ailments; by means of *prāṇāyāma*, he destroys sin; and by means of *pratyāhāra*, he abandons mental afflictions. (109)
Through the concentrations (dhāraṇās), the mind attains steadfastness and consciousness becomes wondrous;
through meditative absorption (samādhi), one attains liberation, having abandoned both auspicious and inauspicious karma.
Withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is proclaimed to be accomplished by twelve rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma); by twelve rounds of withdrawal, auspicious concentration (dhāraṇā) is born.
(360) Twelve *dhāraṇās* are declared as one *dhyāna* by those expert in yoga;
by twelve *dhyānas* alone, *samādhi* is designated. || 112 ||
In samādhi, there is the supreme light, infinite and facing in all directions;
when that is seen, the coming and going of ritual action no longer exists.

He states the fruit of the sixfold yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) individually: "By means of posture" (109); "one goes [to liberation] by means of meditation" (110). He shows that, in comparison to the mastery of posture, breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the other limbs possess twelve times the degree of excellence: "Breath... (111–112). Immediately after the accomplishment of *samādhi*...

He says that the state of having accomplished all that was to be done occurs "in meditative absorption" (samādhau): "This Brahman, whose face is turned everywhere, triumphs—[realizing] 'I am this'. (113)

Through the practice of the Ṣaṇmukhī mudrā, the manifestation of *nāda* occurs: having assumed the bound posture (*bandhāsana*), one restrains the breath by closing the ears, eyes, and nostril-pores with the fingers, or having filled it through the mouth.

Having bound [the breath] at the chest together with the *bahvapāna*, the lord of yogis, whose mind is fixed on that, should hold the deity situated at the crown; thus he attains the equality of the supreme reality (*viśeṣatattva*). || 114 ||
When the sky is reached by the wind, a great sound arises;
this is declared to be the accomplishment of sound (nādasiddhi) regarding bells and other musical instruments. 115.

To the question "By what means is samādhi accomplished?", he says: "Having bound," etc. This means that the yogi, having properly assumed the perfected posture (siddhāsana), having bound the penis in the middle and the pair of feet above and below it, and having filled the breath through the mouth with the six-faced mudrā (ṣaṇmukhīmudrā).
Preceded by the three bandhas, one should fix the mind at the crown of the head, in the thousand-petaled lotus, in the fourth state (turya), or in that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta).

The meaning is that by such concentration (dhāraṇā), the lord of yogis attains equality with the specific principles (viśeṣatattva) and reaches the state of the fourth that transcends all remaining principles. || 114 ||
He states that the perfection of practicing the six-faced mudrā is the manifestation of the internal sound (nāda), saying: "The sky.
This refers to the unmanifested sky delimited by the heart. (115)
The practice of breath is the dispeller of all diseases;
through the proper application of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the destruction of all diseases occurs. For those devoid of breath control, the emergence of all diseases follows. (116)
Hiccups, cough, as well as labored breathing, and pains in the head, ears, and eyes—various diseases such as these arise from the disorder of the vital winds (pavana). 117.
Just as a lion, an elephant, or a tiger becomes submissive gradually, so too is the wind mastered through practice; otherwise, it destroys the practitioner. (118)
One should exhale the breath with steady application, fill it with steady application, and bind it with steady application;
in this way, one shall attain perfection.

He states that the practice of *prāṇāyāma* performed according to the rules is the remover of all diseases, whereas when practiced in a contrary manner, it yields contrary results—thus he says: "By means of *prāṇāyāma*. (vv. 116–117). Since this is so, he further explains that the practice of *prāṇāyāma* yields distinguished results when performed according to the scriptures and in the manner taught by the Guru. Thus he says: [v. 118]...
In the practice of breath control, the withdrawal of the senses is essential:
"The sequential withdrawal of the eyes and other senses from their respective objects—that is called their *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal). (120)
Just as the sun withdraws its radiance at the third period,
so the yogi, established in the third limb, removes mental modification.
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.

Since the senses remain under the sway of their respective objects, how can there be success through practice? To the question of how practice becomes fruitful by withdrawing them from those objects, he says: "Of those wandering... (120). How so?
Regarding the statement that "the withdrawal (pratyāharaṇa) must be performed," he explains this with an illustration,

beginning with "just as" (yathā): Just as the sun withdraws its own radiance at the third period, the evening, so too [should one withdraw the mind] from the distinctions of the gross, subtle, and causal bodies, which are differentiated by the stages of childhood, youth, and adolescence.
Whether by way of the distinctions of *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva*, or by way of the distinctions of ascetics, lovers, and forest-dwellers,

the yogi established in the third limb remains unattached therein; through the realization that Brahman— established by the negation of everything— is his own non-dual self alone, he [renounces] the mind, its modifications such as volition, and so forth.
"Haret" means one should remove, dissolve, or effect a concealment; thus ends the word "Upaniṣad," signifying the completion of the Yogacūḍāmaṇi Upaniṣad. || 121 ||
This clear commentary on the *Yogacūḍāmaṇi* has been written by Upaniṣadbrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra.
The Cūḍāmaṇivivaraṇa consists of two hundred and eighty [verses].
Thus ends the commentary on the Yogacūḍāmaṇyupaniṣad, constituting the forty-sixth [treatise] in the commentary on the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Śrīmadīśa.
